judgements.skipSteelman: measure-refute.js ALREADY has the only breaker that mattered, structurally: at :193-195 a null/thrown measurement returns UNMEASURED and maps LENSES to unverified() WITHOUT calling agent(). measure-refute.test.mjs:53-56 pins it — 3 units, every agent dead, labels.length === 3, not 9. So the 'units x lenses queued behind the wall' the proposal claims to save is NOT spawned today. The residual saving of a streak breaker is the remaining MEASURE agents only (at most UNITS.length - 2), and those are the calls that, after a session wall, return null fast and near-free. The spend that hurt was already gone: SALVAGE.md records 1,369,556 tokens across 28 agents (~48.9k each) burned BEFORE the wall — a breaker trips after the money, never before it. Worse, it cannot tell a wall death from a per-agent death (a bad path in unit.read, an oversized prompt, a schema rejection), so two unlucky units silently abort a healthy 20-unit run. Fit nit: the incident that motivates this cluster did not run through measure-refute.js at all — SALVAGE.md:33 names the script as jclaw-lessons-wf_34d136e7-2d8.workflow.js, an ad-hoc session script that would not inherit any guard added here.
judgements.bittenUsEvidence: Real deaths, yes: SALVAGE.md '25 killed by session limit'; memory records three consecutive-day lane deaths (08-13/14/15) and 10 agents dead after ~687k tokens (07-25). But NO record anywhere shows a breaker changing an outcome — every recovery in the record came from the disk-write rule (SALVAGE.md:3 'the disk kept 5 of 8 studies' while the run's own accounting said 2/8).

judgements.skipSteelman: The probe already exists and costs zero lines: invoke the workflow with one unit. An operator who doubts the credit state runs measure-refute with units.slice(0,1) and looks. Making it default-true taxes EVERY healthy run with a serial agent before the fleet starts — on an ADD-sensitive workflow that is a permanent cost paid for a rare event. The probe is also not representative of what actually dies: UNITS[0] alone proves a single agent can start; the wall is a cumulative session budget that 6 concurrent agents reach and one does not. And the wall announces itself — the round-1 message was 'session limit, resets 8:50pm', a time the operator can read and wait out without any state machine.
judgements.bittenUsEvidence: The three consecutive-day deaths are real, but the countermeasure that recovered value was never a probe — it was write-to-disk-before-returning plus resume-unedited (memory: 'resuming unedited replayed 28 agents free'). judgements.skipSteelman: This is not a fan-out guard at all — it is a maintenance script for dev-server leaks, filed in a cluster about agent accounting. It is also not a GATE: nothing goes red, and its own proposal says it must be 'run from the session-kickoff playbook line' — i.e. it is a written rule with a script attached, which is precisely the weak form this cluster is supposed to be arguing past. It imports a destructive capability into a PUBLIC repo whose users' process trees we cannot see, to fix a failure caused by our own '&' tool calls; the durable fix is not leaking the process, not sweeping up after it. JClaw's own first version of this sweep killed a live test server and cost a 19.5-minute rejected push — the defect it introduces has bitten harder than the defect it prevents.
judgements.bittenUsEvidence: Genuine: ~12 orphaned processes on an 8 GB box (2026-09-10 memory), and the study measured a fresh 2-hour-old http.server leak. This is the one candidate whose underlying problem is unambiguously ours and unambiguously current.

standingCost.testsToAdd: A test that spawns two real detached processes and kills one — the flakiest class of test we could add to a zero-dependency public suite, and CI-hostile.
standingCost.newFailureModes: Killing a live run whose signature matched (JClaw's actual incident). A signature list that silently stops matching after a tool renames its process and then reports 'no orphans' — fail-open, the exact class our own rules forbid. A process-group kill (kill -- -PGID) reaching further than intended when a process was not spawned detached.

judgements.simplerVersion: One READ-ONLY line in the handoff/kickoff playbook: ps -eo pid,etime,command | /usr/bin/grep -E 'vite|http\.server|cloudflared' — the human reads three rows and kills what they recognise. No file, no signature list to maintain, no kill path, no test, no platform surface. That is ~90% of the value at 0% of the risk.
judgements.why: The leak is real and current, so do not drop the problem — but the deliverable that earns its keep is one grep in a playbook, not a killing script in a public repo. Build the listing line; drop --kill, the live-exclusion ancestry walk, and the two-dummy test.

judgements.skipSteelman: build-loop.sh is the ONE spawner that WRITES. JClaw's ceiling guards read-mostly subagents; ours would guard the process that edits and commits the repo, and a hard turn ceiling can cut a cycle between an edit and its commit — leaving the working tree dirty and the invariant 'commit at every checkpoint' broken by the guard itself. That failure is worse than the one being prevented. The premise is also overstated: the brief's own citation shows :41 documents LOOP_MAX_TURNS as 'hung-cycle insurance' and :111 passes it — the knob exists and the operator sets it per run; and the loop already has stop conditions (STOP file, stale-PAUSE presumption, geometric backoff), so 'a node with no stop condition' does not describe it. 80 is a guess with no measurement behind it; the brief does not cite a single cycle's actual turn count.
judgements.bittenUsEvidence: No recorded runaway cycle. The recorded build-loop defect was the opposite — an undiagnosable silent cycle (the 07-12 log), which the exit-code stamp at :99-100 already fixed. Memory also frames build-loop.sh as 'crash insurance only', so the exposure window is small.

Stamp the bound into the cycle header written to loop.log (max-turns=${LOOP_MAX_TURNS:-unset}) — one line, zero truncation risk, and it is the half of the proposal that carries evidence for a postmortem. Then set LOOP_MAX_TURNS at the CALL SITE for unattended overnight runs, where the operator has actually decided to accept truncation.

Stamping the value costs one line and makes every future postmortem able to answer 'what bound was it under', which is the real gap. Hard-defaulting a guessed 80 inside a writing loop trades a hypothetical runaway for a concrete mid-write cut.

judgements.skipSteelman: Fatal calibration problem: the incident is 28 agents; the proposed cap is 48. The guard would have waved the 2026-09-14 disaster straight through. The written rule would not — 8 studies over a repo we did not know breaches the memory's <=6. So on the one case we have, the PROSE is strictly stronger than the CODE. Second, the escape hatch is in the proposal's own done-criterion: '20 units x 3 lenses with maxAgents: 100 -> 80 agents spawned'. Anyone who ignored the rule types maxAgents and proceeds, so this is an arithmetic reminder wearing a refusal's clothes. Third, the caller AUTHORS the units array — the count is not hidden from them the way JClaw's 'already running' count is hidden from a spawning LLM; JClaw's breadth check exists because the caller cannot see concurrent siblings, which does not apply to a single script computing units.length * (1 + lenses.length) from its own argument. Fourth, 48 is arbitrary and boundary-sharp: 12 units x 3 lenses = exactly 48 passes, 12 x 4 = 60 is refused and costs a whole round trip to re-invoke. Fifth, the actual runaway shape was an AD-HOC script (SALVAGE.md:33), which never calls argProblems() at all.
judgements.bittenUsEvidence: The 28-agent / 1.37M-token / 0-lessons run is the most expensive harness failure on record — and it sits BELOW the proposed cap. That is the whole judgement.

judgements.skipSteelman: The CYCLE_RUNNING hazard is reasoned about, not observed: the trap at :51 already clears it on EXIT/INT/TERM, so only SIGKILL or power loss escapes, AND a later session must actually obey the 'wait for it to disappear' header for the stall to happen. streakBreakerWouldHaveHelped.reasoning: Three independent reasons, in order of strength. (1) THE TAIL IT CLAIMS TO SAVE IS ALREADY NOT SPAWNED. measure-refute.js:193-195 returns UNMEASURED for a dead measurement and maps LENSES through unverified() without ever calling agent(); measure-refute.test.mjs:53-56 pins it (3 units, every agent dead -> labels.length === 3, not 9). The proposal's headline saving, 'units x lenses + queued units agent launches per wall', is mostly a saving the file already makes. What a streak breaker adds is suppressing the remaining MEASURE agents — at most UNITS.length minus the deaths already counted. (2) THE BREAKER TRIPS AFTER THE MONEY IS GONE. SALVAGE.md measures 1,369,556 subagent tokens across 28 agents (~48.9k each) and 619,783 ms to the limit. Those tokens were spent by agents doing work, which is WHY the session budget ran out. A rule that reacts to the second death cannot prevent a wall caused by the spend that preceded it, and the agents launched after the wall fail against a session-level refusal, i.e. fast and near-free. So the saving is measured in launches, not tokens. (3) THE COMPARISON WITH THE RULE THAT ALREADY EXISTS IS NOT CLOSE. The disk-write-before-return rule recovered 5 of 8 studies from the same wall — 62% of the run's product, and the only reason 36 candidates exist to be judged at all (SALVAGE.md:3: 'the disk kept 5 of 8 studies' while the run's own accounting said 2/8). A streak breaker recovers zero studies; it improves a label on work that did not happen. If one guard is to be built for wall deaths, the one already built is the right one, and the marginal spend belongs to widening it (every agent writes its JSON before returning) rather than to a spawn gate. TWO HONEST CAVEATS. First, the round-1 run was NOT measure-refute — SALVAGE.md:33 names jclaw-lessons-wf_34d136e7-2d8.workflow.js, an ad-hoc script — so claim (1)'s structural suppression is proven for the file we would be editing, not for the file that died. Second, what would falsify this verdict is one number I was not permitted to read: if the 18 refuters each burned tens of thousands of tokens before dying (rather than failing fast post-wall), the breaker's saving becomes real. That is settled by one command over a file outside my contract: /usr/bin/grep -o '"tokens":[0-9]*' docs/research/runs/jclaw-2026-09-14/journal-wf_34d136e7-2d8.jsonl — run it before spending 25 lines on this.

collapses.intoOneChange: ONE edit to measure-refute.js, ~4 lines, no new control flow: (a) at :192 stop swallowing the error — .catch((err) => ({ __dead: String(err && err.message || err).slice(0, 200) })) and print it in the UNMEASURED integrity string at :195; (b) one log() before phase('Measure') announcing the planned agent count ('N units x (1 + M lenses) = P agents'). That is the whole earned content of three ADOPT candidates: the reason survives a wall, the operator sees the size before it spawns, and nothing new can refuse, trip or under-spawn. Test cost is near zero — measure-refute.test.mjs:144 already drives a throwing measure agent, so its existing assert.match tightens by one regex, and the log assertion needs a log stub the harness already passes.

ONE doc-and-stamp edit to build-loop.sh with zero new logic: stamp max-turns=${LOOP_MAX_TURNS:-unset} into the cycle header line, and change the header's CYCLE_RUNNING instruction from 'wait for it to disappear' to 'a marker older than your session start is stale — delete it and proceed'. Both candidates' value is a postmortem being able to answer a question; neither needs a constant or a liveness probe.
